title: Policies to alleviate poverty and redistribute income

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Set out the policies a government holds against poverty, trace how each works, and weigh strength against drawback.

blocks.heading: The four main policies
blocks.text: To redistribute income is to narrow the gap between the highest and lowest incomes, moving spending power from the better-off to the worse-off. The main policies: progressive taxation, which takes a larger share of income from high earners than from low earners; transfer payments, such as the old-age pension, child grants and unemployment benefits, which put money straight into low-income households; a minimum wage, which sets a legal floor under pay; and direct provision, such as free basic schooling and state healthcare, which gives poor households services they could not buy. Brazil ties family grants to school attendance, and the Netherlands holds pensioner incomes up through transfers - the same levers outside southern Africa.

blocks.heading: A grant traced to the line
blocks.text: Trace a transfer. A household of four in Otavi earns N$2 400 a month, which is N$600 per person, below the absolute line of N$700. The government pays a child grant of N$250 per child a month, and the household has two children, so the grant adds 2 x N$250 = N$500. Household income becomes N$2 400 + N$500 = N$2 900, which is N$725 per person: the grant carries the household across the absolute poverty line. Because the grant is paid for each child in school, attendance tends to rise as well, which works on the weak skills that caused the low income in the first place.

blocks.heading: Strength, and the drawbacks that temper it
blocks.text: Grants work fast and reach households no employer can help - that is their strength. The drawbacks temper them. A poverty trap: as a household earns more, its grants are withdrawn, so the gain from extra work is small and some earners may decide work does not pay. Cost: transfers and free services must be funded from taxation, so a wide programme may strain the budget or force other spending down. The minimum wage has its own limit: where the floor is set above the market wage and demand for that labour is elastic, firms may take on fewer workers, so the policy aimed at the poor may add to joblessness among them.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: The tax system these policies lean on belongs to topic 4.3, and the growth that offers a lasting exit from poverty to topic 4.6.
